name: Adithyapuram Sun Temple
significance: Described as the only shrine in Kerala with Surya as the presiding deity, standing near Kaduthuruthy in Kottayam district. Its tantric rights are held by descendants of the Nambudiri family of Kapikkadu Marangattu Mana.
story: Legend holds that a Nambudiri who meditated on the sun god was instructed by Surya himself to consecrate the idol on this spot.

name: Kidangoor Subramanya Swami Temple
significance: One of the better-known Subramanya shrines in Kerala, on the banks of the Meenachil river. Kidangoor was among the sixty-four Nambudiri settlements lying on the frontier between the Vadakkumkur and Thekkumkur kingdoms, and the site also holds a Vishnu shrine reckoned older than the Subramanya temple.
story: Temple tradition says the Subramanya idol slipped from a sage's water pot and travelled along with the water until it came to rest at the older Vishnu shrine.

name: Sukreesvarar Temple, Kurakkuthali
significance: A Shiva temple on the north bank of the Noyyal river about 8 km from Tiruppur, counted among the Vaippu Sthalams sung by the Nayanar Sundarar. It carries inscriptions of the Cholas, Pandyas and Udayars, in which the deity is named Aludaya Pillai and Milakeesan.
story: Local legend tells of a farmer who cut off the ears of the temple's Nandi; a member of his family was struck mute, and when a replacement Nandi was installed the two figures returned of themselves to their original places.

name: Dhumnath Temple
deity: Shiva, associated with the goddess Dhumesvari
style: Bhumija, with a curvilinear Nagara shikhara
significance: A state-protected Shiva temple at Sargaon raised under the Kalachuris of Ratanpur. Its shrine sits below ground level, reached by six descending steps, and later houses have encroached on the hall and ante-chamber.

name: Sringeri Sharadamba Temple
deity: Sharadamba, a form of the goddess Saraswati
significance: The principal shrine of Sringeri, traditionally founded by Adi Shankara in the 8th century and dedicated to Sharadamba. Pindari raiders sacked it during the Third Anglo-Mysore War in 1791, after which Tipu Sultan wrote to the Sringeri Shankaracharya offering protection, money and gifts to restore it.

name: Manibhadresvara Temple – II
significance: A small rekha deula on the Rath Road running from the Mausima (Ramesvara) temple to Badheibanka Chowk in Bhubaneswar. It now stands abandoned on privately owned land and is cracked on every side.

name: Devasabha Temple
significance: A pancharatha rekha deula inside the Kharakhia Vaidyanath temple precinct in the old town of Bhubaneswar, now abandoned with an empty sanctum. Its name is explained locally as the assembly hall of all the gods and goddesses.

name: Radha Madan Mohan Temple, Vrindavan
deity: Madan Mohan (Krishna) with Radha and the gopi Lalita
significance: A red-sandstone Vaishnava temple about 20 m high, rebuilt in 1580 under the direction of Sanatana Goswami with funds from the Multan trader Kapur Ram Das. The original image was taken to Jaipur in 1670 ahead of Aurangzeb's campaign and later to Karauli under King Gopal Singh; a replica was installed in 1748 and the hilltop temple rebuilt in 1819 by Nanda Kumar Basu.
story: The deity is said to have been found at the foot of an old banyan tree by Advaita Acharya and to have been worshipped by the saint Mirabai.

name: Dolagovinda Siva Temple
deity: Shiva, as a lingam set in a circular yonipitha
significance: Also called the Vaidyanatha Shiva temple, this small Kalingan shrine stands at Rathagada Chowk in the old town of Bhubaneswar. Local tradition credits it to the Kesharis (Somavamsis), though its design does not match that dynasty's usual work; the name comes from the Dola Mandapa across the street.

name: Abhimukeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the eastern bank of the Mahamaham tank at Kumbakonam, one of the twelve Shiva temples linked to the Mahamaham festival held every twelve years. Its most recent consecration was on 26 October 2015.
story: The name is explained by a legend in which Shiva turned to face the nine river goddesses when they arrived, so granting them his darshan.

name: Nandi Temple, Khajuraho
deity: Nandi, the bull mount of Shiva
style: Cross-quadrate plan on a rectangular platform
significance: A Chandela-built pavilion shrine in the Western Group at Khajuraho, part of the UNESCO-listed Khajuraho Group of Monuments. It houses a seated Nandi 2.2 m long and 1.8 m high, facing the Vishvanatha Temple opposite.

name: Kedareshwara Temple, Halebidu
style: Hoysala, soapstone trikuta on a stellate plan
significance: A three-shrine soapstone temple at Halebidu raised between 1173 and 1219 CE by the Hoysala king Veera Ballala II and his queen Ketaladevi. Though Shaiva, its sculpture draws on both Shaiva and Vaishnava themes, and it is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India as a monument of national importance.

name: Karchapeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Kanchipuram built by the Pallavas and later renovated by the Vijayanagara kings, with a rajagopuram, inner gopura and temple tank. It is counted among the Vaippu Sthalams named by the Nayanar Appar.
story: The temple's name comes from the belief that Vishnu worshipped Shiva here in his kurma (tortoise) form.

name: Chitragupta Temple, Khajuraho
significance: The one temple at Khajuraho dedicated to Surya, built about 1020–1025 CE and probably consecrated on Shivaratri, 23 February 1023. Part of the UNESCO-listed Khajuraho Group and an ASI Monument of National Importance, it holds an unusual eleven-headed Vishnu showing his supreme form with the ten incarnations.

name: Paradaresvara Siva Temple
deity: Shiva, represented by a circular yonipitha (lingam missing)
style: Kalingan (laterite rekha deula in dry masonry)
significance: A 13th-century laterite rekha deula in the Gosagaresvara temple precinct on Ratha Road, about a kilometre west of the Lingaraja Temple in Bhubaneswar. Its sanctum retains a three-square-metre circular yonipitha but has lost its lingam.

name: Sanisvara Siva Temple
deity: Shiva, represented by a circular yonipitha
significance: A small pidha deula of the Eastern Ganga period at Kapilaprasad in Bhubaneswar, with a sanctum of about one square metre holding a circular yonipitha. It stands between the Paradaresvara Siva Temple to the north and the Gosagaresvara tank to the west.
story: Local legend says Shiva bathed in the Gosagaresvara pond to cleanse himself after unwittingly killing a calf, and devotees still bathe there for the same purpose.

name: Patalesvara Siva Temple – II
style: Kalingan (sandstone rekha deula in dry masonry)
significance: A sandstone rekha deula on the Talabazar road between the Kedara-Gouri and Lingaraja temples in Bhubaneswar, now partly buried and broken. Water infiltration leaves the deity submerged for most of the year.

name: Patalesvara Siva Temple – III
deity: Shiva, as a lingam in a circular yonipitha
significance: A 13th-century sandstone pidha deula at Mandir Chowk, just east of the eastern gateway of the Lingaraja temple and next to the Mahakala and Mahakali shrines. Its sanctum lies 2.59 m below the present road level and is reached by seventeen descending steps, and its doorway carries Shaiva dvarapalas.

name: Sundaresvara Siva Temple
deity: Shiva as Sundaresvara, in a north-facing circular yonipitha
significance: A rekha deula at Sundarpada in Bhubaneswar dated by its architecture to about the 13th century. Villagers raised funds to install a new Shiva lingam in April 2013 after the old one decayed, and the shrine is run by the Sri Sri Dadhivamana Sundaresvara Mahadeva Trust Board under the state Endowment Department.
story: Local tradition credits the temple to the Kesari (Somavamsi) dynasty and specifically to Yajati I, the builder of the Lingaraja temple.

name: Lakshmi Temple, Khajuraho
deity: Originally Garuda; a Brahmani image installed in modern times is now worshipped as Lakshmi
style: Small sanctum with pillared mandapa on a raised chabutara
significance: A small mid-10th-century shrine in the Western Group at Khajuraho, facing the eastern entrance of the Lakshmana Temple and north of the Varaha Temple. It was raised for Garuda, so the popular name Lakshmi Temple is a misnomer, and its plain outer walls carry no sculpture.

name: Vaithya Lingam Temple
deity: Shiva as Sri Vaithya Lingam Swami (goddess Yogambigai)
significance: A Shiva temple at Aladipatti in Nallur, Tenkasi district, where the lingam is worshipped as Vaithya Lingam Swami alongside the goddess Yogambigai.

name: Uthralikavu Rudhira Mahakalikavu Temple
significance: A small rural shrine of the goddess Kali near Wadakkanchery in Thrissur district, best known for the Uthralikavu Pooram it hosts every February or March. The festival opens with a flag-hoisting on the second Tuesday of Kumbham and culminates seven days later, and is reckoned the second most heavily attended pooram after Thrissur Pooram.

name: Valiyakulangara Devi Temple
significance: A Bhadrakali temple at Mahadevikadu in Karthikappally, Alappuzha district, about 4 km from Haripad. Its principal festival, Aswathi in February or March, is marked by fireworks and Kettukazhcha processions of decorated temple chariots and effigies.

name: Utkanteshwar Mahadev
significance: A Shiva temple on the bank of the Vatrak river in Kapadvanj taluka, Kheda district. Ali Muhammad Khan described it in the 18th-century Persian chronicle Mirat-i-Ahmadi.

name: Uttara Swami Malai Temple
place: Sector 7, R. K. Puram, New Delhi
style: Tamil, Chola style (subsidiary shrines in Pandya style)
significance: Delhi's Malai Mandir at R. K. Puram, whose foundation stone was laid on 8 September 1965 by M. Bhakthavatsalam with Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri presiding; the main temple was consecrated on 7 June 1973. Further mahakumbhabhishekams followed in 1990, 1995 and 2001, and the Adi Sankara Hall opened on 9 November 1997.

name: Valliyoorkkavu Temple
deity: Bhadrakali, worshipped in three forms as Bhagavathy, Vana Durga and Jala Durga
significance: An old goddess shrine near Mananthavady in Wayanad district whose annual fourteen-day festival falls in March and draws large crowds from across the district.
story: The image is held to be self-manifested, and the festival closes with the rudhirakkolam, which enacts the goddess's victory over the demon king Darika.
